Dead or Alive 7 is still being developed, and it doesn’t have a release date at the time of writing. Dead or Alive 6 Last Round received middling reviews on its release in June, with many players — and even our own reviewers at IGN — bemoaning the lack of rollback netcode and lack of cross-platform play on launch, leaving players hopeful that the team at Koei Tecmo will take their feedback into consideration for its next DoA title.

articles.title: Wardogs Surpasses 1 Million Copies Sold on Day One, Blows Past 300k Peak Concurrent Players on Steam
articles.summary: Wardogs has already surpassed a million copies sold and is lighting up Steam's concurrent player charts.
articles.body:
Wardogs has already surpassed a million copies sold and is lighting up Steam's concurrent player charts.

Earlier today, developer Bulkhead launched its brand new all-out warfare FPS, Wardogs. The game has been one of the more highly anticipated shooters of this year and players are showing up for it in force. According to the developer, the game has already surpassed a million copies sold, and SteamDB shows that the game has over 300,000 concurrent players. As a result, a lot of players are being put into server queues, preventing them from getting directly into the action.

“To cross a million copies sold as we launch into early access is mental,” said Joe Brammer, CEO at Bulkhead. “We've spent the last few months showing people exactly what Wardogs is, what it isn't, and at one point literally gave everyone ten reasons not to buy it. We didn't want people buying into blind hype. So seeing more than one million people choose to jump in and play the game at early access launch means a huge amount to all of us. But this is still early access. We've got things to fix, things we want to improve and a lot more we want to build. The best thing players can do now is keep playing, keep telling us what they think and keep giving us those ridiculous Wardogs moments.”

Wardogs is currently only available on PC, making its debut sales numbers all the more impressive, but it is coming to consoles. Bulkhead confirmed that Wardogs is targeting a 2028 release for PS5 and Xbox , but didn't offer a concrete release date. The developer has also noted that it expects the hype to die down eventually, as they plan to take their time when it comes to releasing new content and therefore there may be drops in player counts.

However, it's a strong debut from a new multiplayer shooter. Whether the game can keep players interested to keep returning as new content is added remains to be seen, but it's great to have something other than Call of Duty and Battlefield making an impact. Wardogs attempts to find a unique balance between mil-sims like Arma and something a bit more casual like Battlefield, resulting in a tense, grounded, but large-scale experience filled with emergent moments. So far, players seem to be eating it up and it will likely only continue to grow its audience as word of mouth spreads.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: Top 15 Best Wolverine Comics
articles.summary: Wolverine has been fighting the good fight for decades in the Marvel Universe. These are his 15 greatest comic book storylines of all time.
articles.body:
After all these years, Wolverine remains one of the biggest weapons in Marvel’s vast arsenal. He’s appeared in many thousands of comics. Hugh Jackman’s Wolverine was front and center in Fox’s long-running X-Men movie universe, and he recently made the jump to the MCU in 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine . Looking ahead, we’re expecting Marvel to make good on the promise to keep working Jackman until he’s 90, and the character now makes a grand return to video games in Marvel’s Wolverine on the PS5 .

In light of this renewed Wolverine mania, we’ve extensively updated our list of the best Wolverine comics and graphic novels of all time. Spanning both Wolverine’s solo adventures and Logan-centric issues of books like Uncanny X-Men, these are the comics every self-respecting Wolverine fan must read.

Take a look, then head to the comments to let us know what your favorite Wolverine stories are!

Creative Team: Charles Soule & Steve McNiven

As seen in: Death of Wolverine #1-4 (2014)

We have to hand it to Marvel. They actually had the courage to kill off arguably their most popular character in 2014 and actually let that death stick for several years. And while many of the books connected to Logan’s death and eventual resurrection are better left forgotten, the core Death of Wolverine miniseries from 2014 is pretty great.

In Death of Wolverine, Logan is forced to confront his imminent mortality after his healing factor shorts out. And when Weapon X rears its head once more, the Ol’ Canucklehead embarks on one last gauntlet of foes in order to settle all scores and ensure he leaves the Marvel Universe a better place than he found it.

Death of Wolverine handles Logan’s emotional journey well, in part because writer Charles Soule is so sparing with his dialogue and narration. This series is very much fueled by Steve McNiven’s gorgeous artwork, who manages to top even his legendary work in 2008’s Old Man Logan.

Creative Team: Paul Jenkins & Andy Kubert

For decades, Marvel had slowly been peeling back the layers of mystery surrounding Wolverine's life, but most answers only tended to dredge up more questions. It wasn't until 2001 that Marvel finally went all out and revealed to readers the earliest events of Logan's life.

For starters, Origin revealed that his real name wasn't Logan, but... well, if you don't know, there's no point in spoiling it. Origin paints a tragic picture of a young man whose pleasant family life is torn apart, forcing him to embrace the beast within. Origin shows just how far back many of Logan's defining characteristics extend, from his tendency toward doomed romance to his struggle to suppress his savage nature.

And more than any other Wolverine story, this tale directly influenced 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine. Certain panels from Origin are mirrored almost exactly in the film. Consider Origin a healthy primer for Logan’s cinematic journey.

As seen in: Wolverine: Weapon X #1-6 (2009)

Jason Aaron has long since established himself as one of the greatest Wolverine writers of the modern era, with a years-long run that spans multiple volumes of Wolverine and books like Wolverine: Weapon X. But for our money, Aaron peaked with this early storyline that hit the stands just in time for 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine movie.

In The Adamantium Men, Logan faces off with a mercenary team created in his own image. A PMC called Blackguard gains access to Weapon X’s files, allowing them to create a new breed of super-soldiers equal to Logan in every way - from enhanced senses and healing factors to unbreakable claws. It’s up to Wolverine to prove that he’s still the best there is at what he does and bring down Blackguard by any means necessary.

“The Adamantium Men” works well as a standalone story, but it’s also a great stepping stone into Aaron’s longer run with the character. We hope you survive the experience.

Creative Team: Chris Claremont & Barry Windsor-Smith

Lady Deathstrike is easily one of Wolverine’s most compelling villains. Her hatred for Logan burns as bright as that of Sabretooth, but with the added touch that she believes Wolverine’s very existence perverts the work of her father. Never has that rivalry been better explored than this classic Uncanny X-Men issue.

In “Wounded Wolf,” Yuriko Oyama and her minions transform themselves into deadly cybernetic warriors and attack Logan, leaving him badly wounded and amnesic. It falls on young Katie Power to help our beloved X-Man regain his senses and turn the tables on his attackers. This issue is a great reminder that X-Men comics don’t get much better than when Chris Claremont and Barry Windsor-Smith are working in tandem.

Creative Team: Mark Millar & John Romita, Jr .

As seen in: Wolverine Vol. 3 #20-31 (2004-2005)

In the beginning of the new millennium Wolverine, along with his fellow X-Men, traded in traditional superhero spandex and epic battles for black leather and a more post-modern viewpoint on human/mutant relations. But by 2004, the spandex and supervillains had returned. Mark Millar and John Romita, Jr. helped induct Wolverine back into the realm of bombastic superhero storytelling with "Enemy of the State".

In this tale, Wolverine is brainwashed by HYDRA and The Hand to attack his fellow superheroes. Almost overnight, Wolverine becomes the most feared name in the superhero community. Millar's story allows an unrestrained Wolverine to test his skills against some of the finest the Marvel Universe has to offer. And when he inevitably breaks from HYDRA's control, Wolverine sets out to almost singlehandedly bring down their operation.

This is not the most realistic or grounded Wolverine tale by any stretch. However, it is a lot of fun and helps remind readers that, when he sets his mind to it, Wolverine really is the best there is at what he does.

Analysis: Not to be confused with the 2017 movie, Logan is the sort of deceptively simple story that may not immediately grab you, but by the end of the final issue you realize you just read a true Wolverine classic. Vaughan's tale begins innocently enough. With Wolverine's memories restored following the conclusion of House of M, he returns to Japan to settle some unfinished business. The story follows Logan in both the present and the past as he deals with his time as a WWII POW.

Brian K. Vaughan’s story contains many familiar elements. This is hardly the first time Logan has traveled to Japan to settle old scores. And it's certainly not the first time he's entered into a doomed romance with a pretty Japanese girl. But as always, Vaughan arranges his pieces and executes them near flawlessly.

But as Vaughan himself will readily admit, his real impetus for working on the book was the chance to collaborate with Eduardo Risso. Risso proves himself a master when it comes to Wolverine, crafting a look that falls far from the 100 Bullets tree but rivals anything to come out of that landmark series. When a new reader asks for a Wolverine story light on continuity but heavy on enjoyment, this is what you should hand them.

Creative Team: Chris Claremont & Jim Lee

As time went on, it became more and more apparent that Wolverine's shadowy past extended back untold decades. This issue of Uncanny X-Men peels the curtain all the way back to WWII, offering a classic team-up between Logan , Captain America, and Black Widow.

At a time when the X-Men still existed largely within their own little bubble, it was a treat to see Wolverine interacting with so much of the extended Marvel Universe. Claremont explores more of the character's history in Madripoor, an island that has affected and continues to influence the course of his life.

And, of course, few artists have so defined the modern look of Wolverine more than Jim Lee. Lee was all over the X-Men books in the late '80s and early, early '90s, but this is arguably one of his crowning achievements with the team.

Creative Team: Stuart Moore & C.P. Smith

When the going gets tough, the tough turn to Wolverine to get the job done. This standalone story sees Wolverine traveling to Africa to do a favor for Black Panther. The mission is simple – escort a young girl outside her native country and across the border to safety. Naturally, doing so is much easier said than done.

Stuart Moore truly puts Wolverine through the wringer in this issue, as he suffers one grievous bodily injury after another. Each bullet wound and arrow shot is hammered home by the noir-flavored art of C.P. Smith. As with Ultimate X-Men #41 (more on that book shortly), there is an inevitable sense of tragedy to the mission, but the fact that Wolverine sees it through to the end anyway tells you all you need to know about him.

Creative Team: Peter David & Todd McFarlane

When Wolverine and Hulk first met, the former was assigned by his government to take down the latter. It was strictly business. In this meeting, the lines are not as clearly drawn. In the battle between man and monster, nobody wins.

During this period, Bruce Banner existed as Gray Hulk, a cunning but brutish creature who always lusted for a fight, unlike his greener self. Wolverine, meanwhile, was doing his best to live a life of peace as taught by Xavier. But when you throw these two together in the middle of a snowstorm, watch out. What ensues is one of the most savage and bloody battles the two have ever been caught up in. When the dust settles, both are left to question their own thirst for violence.

Creative Team: Greg Rucka & Darick Robertson

As seen in: Wolverine Vol. 3 #1-19 (2003-2004)

When Marvel relaunched Wolverine’s monthly series in 2003, it came during a time when the X-Men had abandoned spandex and superheroes for black leather and a darker, more experimental tone. Accordingly, Greg Rucka and Darick Robertson came aboard to revamp Wolverine into a grittier and more grounded look at what happens when Logan isn’t on the clock at the Xavier Institute.

The result is easily one of the best Wolverine runs ever published, full stop. And while Sabretooth factors into the third and final story arc, the series is generally concerned with pitting Logan against more ordinary foes like human traffickers and arms dealers. Rucka and Robertson’s Wolverine is basically the franchise’s answer to Punisher MAX, and that should be more than enough reason to give it a look.

Wolverine is no pleasant, easygoing fella' even on his good days. That said, Ultimate Wolverine makes his classic counterpart look like a dainty maiden. Ultimate Wolverine is meaner, angrier, and even more quick to pop his claws when the situation gets hairy. His tendency towards killing takes on a tragic aura in Ultimate X-Men #41.

Though this issue serves as part 2 of a 6-part story arc, it functions perfectly well as a standalone tale. The story opens with a teenage boy who awakes to discover he is a mutant. His power instantly kills anyone who comes close. Nick Fury, not knowing what else to do, dispatches the fast-healing Wolverine to meet with the young man.

Many readers will see the ending coming a mile away. That doesn't rob those final pages of their power by any means. Bendis' script is unusually quiet in this issue, creating one of the most haunting and emotionally effective Wolverine stories ever.

Creative Team: Chris Claremont & John Buscema

There have been and continue to be a lot of great comics focused on the never-ending rivalry between Sabretooth and Wolverine. Are they father and son? Estranged brothers? Members of the same nonhuman species? At this point, you can pick the backstory you like best. But if we were to pick just one comic to showcase this never-ending feud, we have to go with 1989’s Wolverine Vol. 2 #10, by Claremont and John Buscema.

This iconic tale introduces the notion that Sabretooth makes a point of hunting down Wolverine each year on the latter’s birthday to deliver a sadistic “present.” As the story jumps between past and present, readers get a full appreciation for just how deep this rivalry goes, and how much Logan has suffered over the years because of it.

Creative Team: Chris Claremont & Al Milgrom

Issue Span: Kitty Pryde & Wolverine #1-6 (1984-1985)

Claremont and other writers have continuously revisited Wolverine's connections to Japan since the first mini-series, but rarely have these stories been as enjoyable as Kitty Pryde & Wolverine. This unofficial sequel introduces Wolverine's old sensei, Ogun. Readers receive an even closer look at what made Wolverine into the hard-drinking, hard-living warrior he is today.

But as much as this story fleshed out Wolverine, it did even more for Kitty Pryde. Wolverine has had a long history of taking young, female students under his wing. In this story, Kitty evolves from naïve young X-girl to a hardened ninja more confident in her skills. Perhaps Wolverine should have tried the same approach with Jubilee.

This series even inspired an all-ages spinoff called Wolverine: First Class that focuses on this particular Dynamic Duo. If you enjoy First Class and want a slightly harder-edged take on the pair, you would do well to check out First Class.

As seen in: Marvel Comics Presents Vol. 1 #72-84 (1991)

Easily one of the single greatest Wolverine yarns ever spun, no bookshelf is complete without a copy of Weapon X. In 1991, Barry Windsor-Smith delved deep into the Weapon X procedure that morphed Logan the man into Wolverine the killing machine. Rather than look at these events from Wolverine's point of view, Windsor-Smith tackled it from the viewpoint of his captors, including Professor Thornton and Dr. Cornelius.

You may recognize this story from watching X-Men: The Animated Series. You may think you know something of it by watching the X-Men movies. But you haven't seen anything until you read the original account. Windsor-Smith tells a story that is brutally violent, haunting, and a touch surreal all at once.

Creative Team: Chris Claremont & Frank Miller

As seen in: Wolverine Vol. 1 #1-4 (1982)

Once upon a time, it was uncommon for Wolverine to garner much attention outside of the pages of Uncanny X-Men . How the times have changed. Wolverine's first real foray into the world of solo superheroics came with this mini-series courtesy of Chris Claremont and Frank Miller.

Of course, there wasn't much superhero-y about this book. Claremont revolutionized the character by establishing him as a failed samurai in search of redemption. Logan's quest brought him back to Japan for the first time, where he fought against the ruthless Lord Shingen for the affections of his daughter, Mariko. The writing is a bit stilted by modern standards, but there's no denying the impact this story left on the character.

And one area that still holds up today is the tremendous artwork by Frank Miller. As much as Claremont revolutionized Wolverine's character, Miller established a visual tone that countless other artists have tried to mimic.

​What's your favorite Wolverine comic? Cast you vote in our poll and let us know in the comments below:

For more classic comic book picks, check out the Top 27 Batman comics and the Top 28 Spider-Man comics .

Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky .

articles.title: Asa Germann Cast as Angel in Marvel's X-Men Movie
articles.summary: Marvel’s X-Men movie has found its Angel in Asa Germann, best known for his roles in Gen V and Scream 7.
articles.body:
Marvel’s X-Men movie has found its Angel in Asa Germann, best known for his roles in Gen V and Scream 7 .

As per The Hollywood Reporter , Germann had actually auditioned for the part of Cyclops, which eventually went to Kit Connor . He wasn’t out of the running, though, and is now playing the X-Men’s iconic Warren Worthington III (better known by his nickname, Angel).

At 28 years old, Germann joins the ranks of a cast that trends younger, alongside 24-year-old Sadie Sink (Jean Gray), 23-year-old Maya Boyd (Storm), and 25-year-old Inde Navarrette, who was confirmed to play Rogue at Disney’s D23 fan convention last month.

Other confirmed cast members include Samara Weaving as Emma Frost and Christopher Abbott as Charles Xavier, with Adam Driver set to play the part of villain Mister Sinister.

THR states that, although Germann didn’t nab Cyclops, Marvel Studios was so impressed with his audition that they decided to cast him as Angel. This isn't totally new territory for the actor; he’s quite familiar with superhero universes, having played Sam Riordan in The Boys spin-off show Gen V, a character with superhuman strength, stamina, mobility, and hearing, among other traits.

Angel's superpowers are all avian-related, given his wings and all. The character has been a popular topic on social media as of late, with fans remembering a harrowing scene from 2006's X-Men: The Last Stand where he pulled out his feathers as a child.

First appearing in 1963 comic The X-Men #1, Angel was a founding member of the X-Men and an heir to the wealthy Worthington estate. He operated as a vigilante under the name Avenging Angel before joining the group, eventually getting transformed into the brooding Archangel with metallic wings by the hand of Apocalypse.

Marvel's X-Men cast continues to roll out as the months go by, something that Marvel Studios prez Kevin Feige said would happen at D23. By the looks of things, this cast is here to stay, as Feige teased "sagas upon sagas" of stories about the X-Men that "haven't been told" yet.

"Having 85, almost 90 years of comic book history, there's so many stories yet to tell," Feige said. "We announced a very young, new cast for a property called X-Men the other day. And that's great, because there's been 10 great X-Men movies [but] there can be 100 more, " he said at D23's Disney Worldbuilers panel.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: Pay Half Price for the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike Wireless Gaming Mouse With Haptic Inductive Triggers
articles.summary: 10/10 "Masterpiece".
articles.body:
If you're into ultra-light gaming mouse, Logitech's G Pro X2 Superstrike is a top-tier option. It normally commands a hefty price of $179.99, but Amazon Resale is offering used "like new" units for only $90, or exactly 50% off. "Very good" and "acceptable" units are also available for an even lower price, but I generally recommend sticking with the "like new" units if you want a mouse that most likely hasn't been used at all.

Amazon Resale is Amazon's official outlet for used items. Amazon states that this "Like New" item "looks and functions as if it were new and comes in original packaging." You still get the 30-day Amazon return policy so it's a much safer option than buying a used controller off Facebook Marketplace.

50% Off Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike Wireless Gaming Mouse

Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike Wireless Gaming Mouse

IGN's Will Judd reviewed the Superstrike and awarded it a rare 10/10 "Masterpiece" score. This is a "must-have" mouse for competitive players. The Superstrike is the spiritual successor to the Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 mouse. They are both Logitech's lightest mice weighing in at 60 grams with a similar ergonomic shape, they both feature the same Hero 2 sensor, and they have a comparable 40-hour battery life. And that's where the similarities end.

The X2 Superstrike features Logitech's new Haptic Inductive Trigger System (HITS). Instead of physical (and clicky) microswitches, the buttons now use electromagnetic sensors. Logitech claims that this cuts click latency by up to 30ms for phenomenally faster targeting. You'll still feel the click, but it's coming from the haptic motor's rumble, not from the actual click itself. As a side effect, the buttons are quieter, so you can use it at night without bothering anyone, and fewer moving parts means there's less chance for mechanical components to wear out.

Another advantage of electromagnetic sensors is the increased amount of customizability. The X2 Superstrike has tunable action and reset points. You can adjust your click's travel distance, both during the press and the reset. Choose from ten actuation points and five rapid-trigger reset points. This is not dissimilar to the latest generation gaming keyboards with magnetic switches, but it's now translated over to a gaming mouse.

I've actually never seen the X2 Superstrike drop below $100. Granted this deal isn't for a brand new retail boxed unit, but a "like new" one at this price is worth the gamble, especially since Amazon Resale has that solid return policy.

articles.title: PlayStation's Fairgames Seemingly Remerges With First Gameplay, New Codename, and Private Playtest
articles.summary: PlayStation's online heist game, Fairgames, has seemingly re-appeared under a codename with first gameplay and invites to a playtest.
articles.body:
PlayStation's online heist game, Fairgames, has seemingly re-appeared under a codename with first gameplay and invites to a playtest.

Three years ago, PlayStation announced a new online shooter known as Fairgames. It's a competitive heist game, which is a fairly unique concept on paper, but it has reportedly had all kinds of development troubles, including the departure of studio founder Jade Raymond and the game's creative director Daniel Drapeau . Their departures came after staff inside the studio began to express concerns for the game following negative internal playtests. The game has largely gone unacknowledged by PlayStation since its announcement, but development has marched on.

Now, the game has seemingly quitely reemerged under the codename Project Espresso. The game was added to Player.gg , a website that allows developers to connect with players for playtesting. Although the game is under a codename and the developer is being kept under wraps, the listing includes a pretty sizable gameplay trailer which looks strikingly similar to Fairgames. It has a similar art style and concept, and there's a disclaimer that the game is in development for PS5 and PC.

Looks like this is the first official look at gameplay for FAIRGAME$ aka Break In pic.twitter.com/W5KE8nEO9b — Radec (@realradec) September 10, 2026

Looks like this is the first official look at gameplay for FAIRGAME$ aka Break In pic.twitter.com/W5KE8nEO9b

Additionally, the game requires a PlayStation account to be played, something that wouldn't normally happen for a third-party game. It's all a bit odd, but it's hard to imagine it being anything else. And if you're interested in checking it out for yourself, you can sign up for a playtest on Player.gg.

Earlier this year, PlayStation also filed a trademark for a new game known as Break In , which some suspected may be the new title for Fairgames. IGN has reached out to PlayStation for comment regarding the situation and will update the story if we hear anything.

Although Fairgames has been largely shrouded in secrecy, it hasn't stopped gamers from casting doubt on it. PlayStation's other big live-service offering, Concord, was a catastrophic bomb. Additionally, Marathon has failed to impress, The Last of Us Online was canceled, Destiny 2 is no longer being supported, and there's a general disdain for live-service games lately. Outside of PlayStation's first-party offerings, Highguard was meant to be another big live-service title, but was dead within two months.

Fairgame$ PlayStation Showcase 2023 Trailer

Whether Fairgames (or whatever its final name ends up being) can buck trends and get people interested remains to be seen. It's an interesting time for Sony as it navigates nonstop chaos; last night, it was confirmed Hideo Kojima was parting ways with PlayStation after the platform planned to cancel Kojima's ambitious next-gen game, Physint. Xbox stepped in and offered to save it, strengthening the company's relationship with the auteur. Kojima is also developing a new horror game with Xbox known as OD.

PlayStation has also been in hot water with players after its decisions to kill support for physical media in 2028 , shut down Bluepoint a few years after acquiring it, and end support for single-player games on PC . Another live-service bomb would be a big hit to PlayStation's PR right now, so hopefully these playtests can shape it into something appealing to a broad audience.

articles.title: Apple AirPods 5 Are Up for Preorder
articles.summary: Apple AirPods 5 offer active noise cancellation and start at just $129. Preorders are live now.
articles.body:
Announced at the recent Apple event , Apple’s AirPods 5 are set to release on September 18, starting at $129. They’re available for preorder now ( see at Amazon ). These are Apple's latest iteration of its baseline earbuds, the ones without the silicone tips. The biggest new feature is that both AirPods 5 models now have active noise canceling. In fact, Apple says the noise cancellation on AirPods 5 is 50% better than the previous model.

Like previous iterations, AirPods 5 come in two flavors: one with a plug-in charging case for $129, and one with a wireless charging case for $149.

The main difference between the two AirPods 5 models is that the $149 one comes with a wireless charging case, meaning you can charge it on a wireless Qi charger, like Apple’s MagSafe charging disc (which happens to be on sale at Amazon ). The pricier model also has volume control on the earbuds’ stems, which the $129 model does not.

Wireless charging might not sound like a huge improvement, but I find it super useful to charge my AirPods Pro. You just set the AirPods case on it – it sticks via magnets – and let it hang out there until the light turns green (it can also charge an iPhone). It’s a small convenience, but I think it's easily worth the extra $20 to get the model with the wireless charging case.

Whichever model you choose, you’ll get features like spatial audio and Apple’s live translation. AirPods 5 can also automatically switch between transparency mode and noise cancellation mode, depending on what’s going on with the background noise.

As I mentioned above, I own a pair of AirPods Pro, and I use them daily and love them dearly. I actually lost my first pair, and I immediately ran out to buy a second pair because I couldn’t live without them. If you don’t like the silicone tips on the AirPods Pro, or you want a cheaper alternative, AirPods 5 look like an excellent choice – and they're out just next week.

In other news, you can also preorder other newly announced Apple products , including Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Preorders are coming soon for the iPhone Duo, as well as iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

articles.title: Legendary Voice Actor Mike McFarland Dies at 56 Years Old
articles.summary: Legendary voice actor Mike McFarland has died aged 56, leaving behind an indisputable legacy with hundreds of roles across some of the most iconic anime series ever made.
articles.body:
Legendary voice actor Mike McFarland has died aged 56, leaving behind an indisputable legacy with hundreds of roles across some of the most iconic anime series ever made.

News of McFarland’s death broke in the late hours of September 9, 2026. The actor was best known for being the voice of Dragon Ball ’s Master Roshi, Jean Kirstein in Attack on Titan , Buggy the Clown in One Piece , Jean Havoc in Fullmetal Alchemist , and many, many other characters.

If you’re an anime fan, you’ve likely heard McFarlane’s name come up at some point. His career began in the late '90s with the Dragon Ball series, later spanning into other prominent shows like YuYu Hakusho (Komada, Butajiri) and Fruits Basket (Risu Soma).

In August 2025, McFarland was diagnosed with Glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. His fellow voice actors banded together to create a GoFundMe to help raise money for his medical costs, with the likes of J Michael Tatum (Sebastian Michaelis, Erwin Smith) posting about the subject on Twitter/X.

A slew of high-profile voice actors, industry veterans, and fans have spoken out in the wake of his death.

“Mike McFarland, my dear friend and mentor of over twenty years, is gone. A rarer, more beautiful soul this world will never know. Rest in peace, Salt. The love you created endures, but damned if I know how we’ll get on without you around to share it back with,” Tatum wrote.

articles.title: Paul Walker's Brother Suggests AI Could Bring Back Brian O'Conner for Fast and Furious Finale
articles.summary: Cody Walker says AI could be used to bring back Paul Walker’s Brian O’Conner for the Fast & Furious finale if the late actor's daughter Meadow Walker approves.
articles.body:
Vin Diesel has long stated his hope to somehow bring back the character of Brian O’Conner in Fast Forever, but if it does happen it will be without the assistance of late actor Paul Walker’s brothers this time around.

After Paul Walker died in a car accident in 2013 while Furious 7 was in production , his brothers Cody and Caleb Walker (along with actor John Brotherton ) were used as doubles during the remainder of the shoot. Visual effects were then used to map Paul’s likeness over the stand-ins.

Chatting with Entertainment Weekly , Cody Walker said neither he nor Caleb will do that again for what’s been touted as the final film in the Fast and Furious franchise . Instead, Walker suggested artificial intelligence could be used this time to bring Brian back.

“My stance is, it’s what Meadow [Paul’s daughter] wants to see done; it’s her father,” Cody said. ( Meadow Walker cameoed in Fast X and Vin Diesel even walked her down the aisle at her wedding .)

“I would not be interested in doing that again. I love the way his character exited the franchise. They didn’t kill him off, they didn’t do something cheesy like that. It’s beautiful, [Brian] is off raising his kids,” Cody said.

“But if they want to do that, if Meadow would like to see that, they don’t need me or Caleb. AI was not a thing back in 2014, so they could do that. There’s years of footage that was never used from these other Fast films. They’re the best in the business, they can figure that out.”

The Walker brothers previously said back in 2018 that they were hopeful there was a way the series could bring back Paul’s character even though earlier reports suggested the franchise would simply retire the character of Brian O’Conner. But as fans of the franchise know, that isn’t quite what ended up happening.

Ranking the Fast and the Furious Movies: From Worst to Best

Fast 9 director Justin Lin confirmed that Brian O’Conner is still alive in the Fast universe . At the end of Furious 7, Brian and his girlfriend Mia Toretto (Jordana Brewster) flee the outlaw life in order to raise their children in safety. And while the specter of Walker looms over the subsequent Fast & Furious films, and Brian and Mia have been mentioned, the series avoided directly bringing Brian back … until the very last scene of Fast 9 .

In Fast 9, Mia rejoins big brother Dom (Diesel) and the crew to track down and stop their renegade agent brother, Jakob (John Cena). Mia tells Dom that Brian is looking after his namesake, Dom’s toddler son Brian, and their own kids while she’s on this mission. In the end, the crew convenes for a family dinner at Dom’s home in L.A. There's an empty chair with Mia telling Dom that its occupant is on their way but running late. That’s when the scene cuts to a familiar blue car, a Nissan Skyline driven by Brian in past movies, pulling into the driveway before cutting to black. While we never see the driver, the implication is clear: Brian O'Conner is back with his family.

Diesel has made it clear that he feels it's important for the story and fans to bring back Brian O’Conner one last time for the saga’s finale, which he said will see the franchise return to its street racing roots . “I couldn’t imagine this saga ending without truly saying goodbye to Brian O’Conner," Diesel told Total Film in 2023.

In January, Diesel announced the release date and title for the sequel to Fast X in an Instagram post using a photo of his and Walker’s characters in the original 2001 film: "No one said the road would be easy… but it’s ours. One that has defined us and become our legacy… And a legacy… lasts Forever. March 17th 2028! FAST FOREVER."

Fast Forever will be directed by Louis Leterrier, who also directed Fast X , which opened to poor reviews and proved to be the lowest-grossing entry in the franchise .

Fast X also shocked fans by bringing back Dwayne Johnson’s Luke Hobbs and Gal Gadot’s Gisele Yashar in cameos that clearly set them up as returning for the next and final film. Time will tell if that indeed happens.

articles.title: This Week's Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Is a Tale of the Once and Future Captain Kirk... and It's a Good One!
articles.summary: In Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 8, “Orders of Magnitude,” Joe Morton is terrific as that classic style Trek guest star – the visiting Admiral who takes command of the ship – while Paul Wesley gets to deepen his take on the James T. Kirk that we know he’s evolving into.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 8, “Orders of Magnitude.”

And now we’re back to regular Star Trek again with this episode, after weeks of “concept” stories . “Orders of Magnitude” isn’t doing any gimmicks, even if it is trading on a tried-and-true set-up that Trek itself has tackled itself many times before – that of the increasingly erratic and dangerous commander whose questionable decisions put his crew into a moral quandary.

While Captain Pike (Anson Mount) and his away team are planet-bound and out of communications range, the legendary Admiral Simon Reeger (Terminator 2’s Joe Morton!) shows up in a shuttlecraft and announces that he’s taking command of the Enterprise. He’s uncovered a way to track a mysterious, cloaked enemy vessel that is believed to be responsible for something known as the Vardan Massacre, which resulted in 5 million civilian casualties. (The way he’s tracking it? The gamma ray burn-off from the ship’s impulse engines, obvs.) But time is of the essence, and so he takes command of the Enterprise while the trail is still hot.

Coincidentally – or not really, since this guy stops by the Enterprise all the freaking time – Lt. Commander James T. Kirk (Paul Wesley) not only happens to be onboard, but his oft-mentioned/never-seen (in this universe anyway) father George Kirk used to be Admiral Reeger’s First Officer during the Klingon War, back when Reeger was the captain of the USS Constitution. It was in that conflict, during the Battle of Zeta Reticuli, that Reeger gained fame as a war hero, while the elder Kirk’s career apparently hit a roadblock. And wouldn't you know it, but as the ranking officer onboard after Reeger, Lt. Commander Kirk must take the temporary post of First Officer for this emergency mission.

Morton is good as Reeger, a guy who immediately commands respect and awe as soon as he walks into a room. The crew of the Enterprise hero-worship this guy, so much so that even as his plan to take out the enemy ship becomes increasingly questionable, they’re willing to follow his orders. (Well, most of them are.) Morton gestures with his hands and puts emphasis on certain words in such a way as to both make his character seem like he knows his shit , but also have us wondering if maybe he’s a little… well, cracked?

And that becomes the question at the heart of this episode. As I noted earlier, we’ve seen variations of this story on Star Trek before – in some of the best Star Trek, in fact. Who can forget Commodore Decker’s doomed face-off against the planet killer in TOS’ “The Doomsday Machine,” or the tragedy in TNG’s “The Wounded” of Captain Ben Maxwell, who never got over the loss of his family in the Cardassian War and almost brought the Federation into another war as a result? Indeed, we eventually learn here that Reeger’s family were among those 5 million lost in the Vardan Massacre.

But does that justify the Admiral wanting to take out the 5,000 people on the planet where the mystery ship is hiding? A ship capable of killing millions? Kirk can’t get his head around it, and this puts him on the outs with Reeger, just as his father fell out with the man all those years earlier on the Constitution. We eventually learn that even though George Kirk was the one who actually stepped up in that battle, it was Reeger who got all the glory. And that’s just how history played out, like it or not, fair or not.

Wesley has grown into the Jim Kirk role, or I’ve grown into accepting him as this version of Kirk at least, and here his unwillingness to just roll over and pull the trigger feels very in line with the character. It also has the unfortunate result of painting the rest of the crew in something of a poor light, as they’re apparently so blinded by their devotion to the Great Admiral Reeger that, sure, they might not love the idea of wiping out 5,000 potentially innocent souls, but they are willing to do it – even Spock!

This leads to the biggest disappointment of the episode, which is the cordrazine cop-out, as I’ll call it. That Doctor M’Benga (Babs Olusanmokun) claims he drugged his old captain (turns out he was on the Constitution back in the day too!) only for us to then find out that actually it was Kirk who drugged him – thereby driving him to the point of paranoia and aggression so that the rest of the crew were finally willing to relieve him of command – means that we never really get a straight answer as to whether or not the attack should’ve proceeded as Reeger had planned. The Enterprise crew took the easy way out on this one, alas.

Meanwhile, over on what is as close to a Planet Hell set that we get on this show (and I love it), Pike and his away team have a decent little adventure with some Orion pirates that gives Uhura (Celia Rose Gooding) the chance to spread her action wings. She also gets a promotion and learns a valuable lesson when the cadet she’s been mentoring, the Vulcan A'Sha (Bianca Nugara), decides to leave Starfleet. As Pike tells Uhura, you can do everything right and sometimes things still don’t work out in the end. That’s the same thing that happened to Kirk’s father, but somehow it feels like the storyline with Reeger might’ve had a more interesting resolution if that lesson was more cleanly applied there as well.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

The Vardan Massacre, eh? Who could the villains be who were behind such a terrible act? And will we learn more about them this season?

Cordrazine, lest we forget, was the drug that Doctor McCoy got all amped up on in the classic Star Trek: TOS episode “The City on the Edge of Forever,” where he went back in time and inadvertently caused Hitler to conquer the world. (Long story.)

The USS Constitution as flagship of the fleet has long been posited and assumed in books, comics, and technical manuals, but this is the first onscreen confirmation of that fact.

Not to get too nerdy here [pushes up glasses], but the D7 Klingon cruisers mentioned here as having faced off with the USS Constitution in the war is a continuity error, since we know that class of ship wasn’t introduced until after the war (as seen in Star Trek: Discovery’s second season ).

And speaking of the war, I may have said this before, but I appreciate how Strange New Worlds is willing to delve into the specifics of the Klingon War in a way that Star Trek: Discovery – which freaking started the war! – stopped doing pretty early on. Of course this would’ve been a key part of many of these characters' early lives and it absolutely should not be ignored.

Whatever happened to Lt. Jenna Mitchell (Rong Fu), who would sit next to Ortegas at the helm console? I don’t think we’ve seen her once this season.

The relationship between Jim and Sam Kirk, on the other hand? I do like it.

La’an likes caves but doesn’t love caves.

articles.title: Call of Duty's Anti-Cheat Boss Dispels Cheating Myths, Breaks Down Review Process, and More
articles.summary: Cheating in video games has turned into a multi-billon dollar industry, which has forced franchises like Call of Duty to build entire teams to combat this epidemic.
articles.body:
Cheating in video games has turned into a multi-billon dollar industry, one that has forced franchises like Call of Duty to build entire teams to combat this epidemic. One of the people leading the charge is a man named David Andrews, a former Department of Defense contractor and member of the Air Force who made the leap into the video game industry. He began this career change working at Rockstar Games, helping combat cheating in Grand Theft Auto Online. Last year, he made the jump to Activision to become the Senior Director of Game Security for Call of Duty.

IGN had the opportunity to sit down with Andrews and peel back the layers on Call of Duty's anti-cheat system, Ricochet. Andrews disspelled myths about Call of Duty's anti-cheat, offered clarity on the process of how they investigate suspected cheaters, how they've hired cheater makers to combat the problem, and much more. It's a rare opportunity, as there's a lot of caution around publicly speaking about anti-cheat in gaming. If you say too much, you could inadvertedly give cheaters a heads-up on how to evade detective, after all.

With that said, we drilled down on Call of Duty's long running issue with cheaters in an attempt to make it less mysterious. It's an important subject ahead of Modern Warfare 4's release in October and something Activision is working hard to spotlight.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

IGN: Before we dive specifically into Call of Duty, tell me the difference between working on Grand Theft Auto Online, Red Dead Online, and Call of Duty, because one's obviously hyper-competitive, while Grand Theft Auto is a completely different ecosystem.

David Andrews: I think the interesting pivot for me is that the GTA Online gameplay loop is very different. Same thing for Red Dead Online, and that's where cheat developers tend to go. They're trying to shortcut whatever that gameplay loop is for their customers. And so on GTA and Red Dead, it was much more about economic progress within the world. So we had problems with money drop lobbies and things like that in the old bad days on GTA Online, which we did eventually fix. The nature of the cheating is different there. In terms of the impact and the disruption that it can cause to the players, very similar.

[There are] persistent online sessions in GTA Online versus rolling lobbies on Call of Duty. A cheater that goes undetected for too long is going to have an impact no matter what that is. There was also lots of griefing in GTA Online powered by cheats and things like that. As different as the core gameplay loops are between the two games, and you could probably say this about anything across the industry, cheating is still just ultimately super disruptive. It's a terrible experience. It's bad for our players, and the mission is always just to try to prevent as many of them as we can from getting into the game and then get them out as quickly as we can for those that make it through.

IGN: Is there something that companies can do together to solve these issues? I saw you last night talking about Wardogs and their approach. Everyone has a different strategy, but is there anything the industry can collectively do?

David Andrews: There's a ton of overlap that we see within the industry. It is an industry-wide problem. If anybody running a live service title is going to have this kind of issue with cheating, and no matter how advanced or what your particular approach is for a particular title or whatever you're doing, cheaters are always going to get through. I thought that a really good message from that Wardogs video was that no matter how good you are at this part of the game, people are going to get through. Cheat developers are incredibly financially incentivized. It's a multi-billion dollar industry out there selling cheats, and they're all looking for their cut of it. I think in terms of what we can do as a group, we definitely all talk with each other informally, always trading war stories and maybe some approaches in terms of what's going on.

Certainly I've seen in my past at Rockstar as well as here at Activision, you'll have cheat developers and cheat resellers out there that are selling not just for one title. There's very rarely somebody who's just developing for Call of Duty. They might have their fingers in Fortnite or Valorant or some other title out there, as well. There's usually opportunities for us to compare notes a little bit whenever that's possible for us to do. By and large though, we all keep pushing forward in terms of all of the things that are available to us. Different companies have different litigation strategies and things like that, but we're all marching in the same direction as much as we can.

IGN: What have you learned about cheatmakers? What’s the motive? It’s hard to wrap my head around why someone would pay $70 for a game just to not really play it.

David Andrews: Money is totally a huge motive for quite a lot of them, but there are also a strain of cheat developers, or I even call them cheat development-adjacent folks, who are just in it for the love of the game. They just really love that title and they have a technical sort of bent of mind and they want to understand how the game is working. And then that naturally leads into this place where you might be putting together a cheat to figure out ‘How does this game actually work?’

And in that space, I've had some success in turning some of those cheat developers or cheat-adjacent people to the light side by basically, bringing them over, and hiring them into the team. They bring a huge expertise and a really unique point of view to add to the team, and it can be a really huge value add for us. We've done that successfully a few times.

I think for their users, the motivation is like you mentioned: You pay $70 or whatever it is for a title just to not play it. It's because they want to be seen to be good and they're not actually good at this game. They kind of suck, which is fair enough. I'm not the best at Call of Duty myself personally, but I wouldn't turn to a cheat to go try to do something about that. But they are in friend groups, they're in social circles that really highly prize competency at these games. And so they go out and this is their only option to be any good at them, so they go out and buy cheats.

IGN: I’d love some insight into the cat-and-mouse game, since there’s a whack-a-mole situation that likely happens with trying to stomp out cheatmakers. There will always be cheaters, regardless of the steps you take.

David Andrews: The main mission is always just to protect the integrity of that live legitimate player experience, just making sure that they're having the best possible experience the way that our game developers intended for them to have. We do that a lot of different ways. The cat-and-mouse game is absolutely part of this, and there's some balancing efforts that go in there, in terms of figuring out when's the right time to ban a cheater once you've detected them. I think in the past, quite a lot of us in the industry indexed pretty heavily towards ban waves for a variety of reasons. One of them is that if you catch enough of the cheat customers in one big roundup, you might knock that cheat offline for a period of time and you actually get more clean running than you would otherwise by just issuing bans as you get them.

That's certainly where I started out philosophically, but as the years have gone on, I don't necessarily believe that that's the most effective way anymore. I think the most effective way is shifting left, preventing cheaters from getting into the game and then once they get into the game, getting them out as quickly as possible. Every single ban that we do gives feedback to the cheat developers and it helps them troubleshoot their problem, which is how did we detect them? It gives them feedback on how to circumvent us, but then that's just a challenge for us to get better at our jobs and do a better job of creating new detections, creating new novel ways of finding cheaters, preventing them and getting them out of the game.

There are a lot of conspiracies about cheating in Call of Duty, such as maybe the perception of how bad it really is due to viral clips. From your perspective, what are some of the myths of the cheating situation in Call of Duty?

David Andrews: I think you've touched on one there. The numbers that we see internally remain really, really positive. We shared during the Black Ops 7 beta that we had a very, very low match infection rate. That's maintained over the course of the title. It's incredibly low. If you're an average player and you're in ranked or you're in Warzone, you're doing whatever you want, you're not encountering a lot of cheaters. But [if] you go on social media and [watch] content creators and pros, they're having a different experience to what you're probably having, and then you're sort of internalizing that. You're seeing, ‘Well, my favorite streamer is encountering cheaters every day.’ I go online, I see something unfair or something inexplicable that I'm not quite sure what happened there. I'm just going to assume that's a cheater as well because I've seen this around. It just doesn't tend to be true for our average players.

Our match infection rate is incredibly good still, but that does still highlight for us that there are hotspots. There are problem areas. We don't want to try to go out there and say ‘We've solved cheating, you're never going to see a cheater.’ Certainly content creators and pro players that are playing at the very tip top edge of ranked play are going to encounter more cheaters right now. We're working on it all the time to try and get them out of the game.

That's the biggest one I think right now. Perception is just quite prevalent that there's a huge cheating problem. It's not to say there is no cheating problem. Obviously Ricochet still exists. We're all still gainfully employed and we're still trying to work on this problem, but it's certainly taken a pretty giant step forward with Black Ops seven with the introduction of TPM and Secure Boot requirements, and we're looking to just keep making more steps forward in the next title.

I wanted to ask a little bit about the review process. So, say I'm suspected of cheating. I've been reported and you guys are going to take a look at my account. What does that look like? Is there a human reviewing it? Is it AI-reviewed? And how long do they spend looking at that? Because I imagine there are a lot of reports. So, how do you sift through that to make sure you guys are giving its due diligence?

David Andrews: I'll say that things come in from a variety of different directions, and the vast majority of our bans that go out are through reviewed but automated systems. So for instance, for a particular cheat, we might deploy a signature that identifies like, ‘Oh, in running memory, if you see this string, this string only exists for this cheat.’ And then we fire that back and we'll collect that data for a little bit on all those accounts that are triggering that detection, look at them en masse, and also one by one and just make sure that those really do look like cheaters. That process is pretty involved.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Screenshots (August 2026)

We look at game data, we have everything that you input into the game clients while you're in a match. All of that data is with us and so we can identify clear outliers there. We also look at trends and behavior, like what is your kill death ratio over time? Does it spike in certain circumstances? What's your win-loss ratio? Things like that. We also will look at replay renders. We have tooling internally that we can just recreate an entire match and look at it and see if it looks suspicious or not. These are just some of the tools that we have internally. So we'll apply that to that whole batch, that whole population of potentially detected cheaters. And if it passes through that validation stage, then we'll say, ‘Okay, that signature is good. People that are popping that signature are going to get banned from now on.’ There's also things that are more manual. All the same tools kind of apply.

We'll still look at the account holistically. We'll look at it per match. We'll look at it in terms of how often they are being reported. All these kinds of data points are valuable to us and then we'll make a determination. That's kind of the stuff that you might see if a social media clip is posted and they aren't already banned. These are the things that we start looking into to see, ‘Okay, well what's going on with this account? What do their last few matches look like? Let's try to make a determination here.’

IGN: There was an incident a week or two ago with a former COD pro player named FormaL, and he triggered the detection in the Modern Warfare 4 beta. Call of Duty’s social team said that wasn’t supposed to happen. Do you know what happened there? What is the percentage of people being banned that shouldn't be banned, and what's the process of making sure that doesn't happen?

Former Call of Duty pro and legend FormaL got permanently banned in the Modern Warfare 4 beta live on stream 💀 The Oris is so good it’s got pros getting their accounts flagged 🤣 pic.twitter.com/8MlHBfbH3G — ModernWarzone (@ModernWarzone) September 2, 2026

Former Call of Duty pro and legend FormaL got permanently banned in the Modern Warfare 4 beta live on stream 💀 The Oris is so good it’s got pros getting their accounts flagged 🤣 pic.twitter.com/8MlHBfbH3G

David Andrews: So, the thing I'll say for that one is I think, obviously, we replied to that particular instance, but he certainly wasn't the only person that was caught up in that slight error there. Betas are for us, as well. We're constantly kind of tuning and testing our systems and transitioning from Black Ops 7 to Modern Warfare 4. There's a lot of tuning that has to take place there to make sure that all of our behavioral thresholds are accurate.

Also, someone like that player is quite high, and so very highly skilled players are kind of constantly brushing up against the threshold where we say ‘Beyond this, no human could achieve that.’ So they're just right there. They're quite close. And so we constantly are looking at this. The answer to the question is really, we're constantly reviewing the output of our systems. We don't just do that review one time and then we set it and forget it.

We're constantly looking back to see, ‘Is this thing still performant?’ Because also we want to know that we're still catching cheaters, but also is it overperforming? Is it catching people that it shouldn't be catching? We've built quite a lot of safeguards over the years. One of the things that impressed me coming in [is that] if there's some conjunction of events where a false enforcement is issued, we tend to catch it fairly quickly and then we will kind of identify systematically who were all the people impacted.

So in that one, it was one of about 200 people, I think, that were caught over the course of both beta weekends with that particular problem. We identified the problem, which won't happen again, and we restored all those people to good standing. So it's just constant review, constant monitoring, always looking at what's going on.

Do you have any involvement with the videos of process servers showing up to people’s houses to give them a cease and desist, or are you just enjoying them?

David Andrews: I certainly enjoy it for sure. I think that we do have a pretty comprehensive grasp on everything that's going on within the cheat community, and that extends to trying to identify devs and potentially put together actions like that. We don't necessarily initiate litigation or send cease and desists to everybody. There is some prioritization and triaging that has to happen. We do go after popular cheats obviously, but we also go after cheats that are technologically sort of more advanced than other cheats as well. And for these incredibly persistent cheat developers who are, again, just enormously financially incentivized, it kind of doesn't matter how often we detect them sometimes. And they'll gaslight their own customers into thinking like, 'Oh, it was you. It was your behavior and game that got you banned. It's not my cheat that got you banned.' And so when they're that stuck in, they're that persistent, they're that sticky, we have to do things like that and certainly the team helps contribute to that.

IGN: I would love to know your stance on how you guys are supporting older Call of Duty games, as cheaters are out there taking advantage of the fact that nobody's really watching them because they're older games.

David Andrews: Yeah, that's unfortunately one that I won't be able to answer.

Editor’s note: Activision linked IGN to a statement recently provided to Windows Central regarding an update that patched out a security issue with the original Modern Warfare 2. The statement notes that more support updates for older Call of Duty games are coming soon: "An update released this week addressed all known vulnerabilities in Modern Warfare 2. The team continues to support our legacy titles, with additional updates coming soon. We encourage anyone aware of additional issues to report them through Activision's Bug Bounty Portal."

How has cheating evolved since you started at Rockstar? We talked about the difference in games, but how have you seen the industry evolve? Has the financial incentive only increased over time, especially as free-to-play games get introduced?

David Andrews: Anytime you're dealing with a free-to-play title, the barrier of entry is just so much lower and that means a broader player population, that means more demand for that title, and more incentive. It’s definitely grown over the years. I think from my particular perspective, the sophistication of the cheat developers is definitely growing as well. [Cheat developers have] their own sort of, we call it OPSEC, operational security, in terms of protecting their identity, because they know what they're doing is not right and they know that the publisher or developer is going to come after them eventually.

So they're getting better and better at hiding themselves from us and working through intermediaries. It’s quite a complex, very interesting sort of threat landscape for us. At the end of the day, it's really evolved over the years. The other thing that's really evolved is cheats used to be pretty simplistic.

They're just hooking, running memory and doing X, Y, Z thing and figuring out what function does what, modifying those functions, and then off to the races. Everybody's anti-cheats have sort of very much pushed them out of the more traditional easy or straightforward ways of cheating. That's why you're seeing growth in other areas like Cronus and other scripted input devices, computer vision powered aim bots, DMA cheats, things that are either reduced in functionality or more expensive, or sometimes both, than what they used to be. The price of a cheat is definitely going up over the years as we all get more and more effective and fight them more consistently.

IGN: Obviously there's software, but there's also hardware like Cronus, physical things that you can purchase. I think Call of Duty has done a pretty good job of trying to stomp that one out, as well as hard platforms in general, like Xbox and PlayStation. How are you guys combating that kind of stuff? It's probably pretty frustrating to know that there's just stuff being sent out in the mail to people. They're just selling it right there. It's not even really hidden.

David Andrews: Cronus and other scripted input devices like that are a really interesting challenge for us. At the end of the day, they do have sort of reduced functionality versus a full blown sheet. So they're usually taking advantage of things like aim assist and just giving it to you all the time or more accurately or whatever.

But absolutely the fact that you can just buy one at a big box store, you can buy one off of any popular online storefront that you might think of, have it shipped to your house and plug it in, and then you're sort of off to the races is definitely frustrating. It also means we've adjusted our enforcement strategy against Cronus as well. It's not the typical enforcement strategy that we have in other places, because we know that for some percentage of these users that are buying a Cronus and plugging it in and getting the advantage off of it, they may not fully realize that that's unauthorized hardware and that it's going to get them banned.

We've actually taken an enforcement stance of, on a first strike, we'll give you a seven-day temporary suspension. We're letting you know you can't use that thing. If you use it again, you're gone forever. And then on a second strike, we catch you using it again, we do permanently suspend that account and there might be implications for your hardware as well, if it's a console or PC or whatever.

We've actually seen pretty good results off of that. We're seeing some rehabilitated behavior. We've certainly gotten some interesting support tickets in that are like, 'I promise I threw away my Cronus. I'll be a good player now. Please let me back in,' that kind of thing, which has been really gratifying to see. The numbers back it up, some percentage of them, which hopefully we can talk about in the future, but some percentage of them are sort of rehabilitating. They take that seven-day suspension and then we don't see any evidence of suspicious gameplay again, which is great. That's where we want to be. For the rest of them, they get permanent bans, they get console or hardware banned, and that's that.

IGN: Is shadow banning a real thing? And what is the argument for why shadow banning works over a permanent ban?

David Andrews: We have limited matchmaking that we will put a suspicious account into to isolate them while other checks are either running or we're waiting on other data. We're kind of doing this review process of looking at that account more holistically and seeing what's really going on here. It's kind of this stopgap measure to immediately remove them without making it be permanent [or without creating] irrevocable impact to that account and to that player, giving us some breathing room to figure out what is going on with this account and then either restoring them to the player population because it was kind of a false alarm situation."

We have also done some rehabilitation through the limited matchmaking saying, 'Hey, you can't do that behavior that you've just been engaged in and you can come back if you stop,' or whatever. We have a lot of enforcement capabilities. We have limited matchmaking, we have ranked play bans, we've got remote play bans, we've got temporary and permanent account suspensions, we've got hardware bans.

We can do all kinds of things, and each time we're dealing with a particular style or type of cheating, we're sort of evaluating which one of these kind of makes sense for this group of cheaters. Can they be rehabilitated? Are we ultimately 100% confident in this? Is more research required? Whatever the case might be, we'll figure out what to do that's appropriate.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Campaign Screenshots

IGN: Anything else you want to get off your chest?

David Andrews: Well, recently, we did a bit of a hiring highlight, and back to the point of hiring cheat devs, we collect people from a wide variety of different talent pools. We've got people on the team that are former malware research engineers, theoretical mathematicians. We've got people from the NSA and FBI on the team doing other sorts of work for us. It's a really interesting space to me. Something that doesn't get talked about a lot is the anti-cheat part of the video game industry, because there are no degrees in this stuff. There are no certifications. It's not been commoditized in that way yet, and so you have to reach out and find interesting talent and really bright and passionate people from different parts of different industries altogether and then bring them into games and be like, 'Yeah, now we're going to go chase cheaters around and get them out of Call of Duty now.'

It's an interesting thing. We're always looking for new, interesting talents, no matter what the background is there, constantly growing people ourselves in these roles. It's a really cool part of the industry to be in.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: 'They Are Alchemy' — Guillermo Del Toro Speaks Out on AI in Filmmaking and Why It Can't Replace Human Creativity
articles.summary: Acclaimed filmmaker Guillermo Del Toro spoke out about his thoughts on artificial intelligence and what he feels gets lost in the creative process when AI is used.
articles.body:
Acclaimed filmmaker Guillermo Del Toro spoke out about his thoughts on artificial intelligence and what he feels gets lost in the creative process when AI is used in art.

Del Toro popped into the r/movies subreddit for an AMA session with fans on September 9. One of these fans, going by the username ihs25ysf, asked him about some comments he’d made during a 2024 talk at the British Film Institute, where he said that AI can create “semi-compelling screensavers” and “that’s essentially that.”

“The value of art is not in how much it costs and how little effort it requires," he said at the time. "It's how much would you risk to be in its presence."

Guillermo Del Toro on AI, emotion and the value of art. Watch the full In Conversation on our YouTube channel. @RealGDT pic.twitter.com/XxO05Fpea7 — BFI (@BFI) September 17, 2024

Guillermo Del Toro on AI, emotion and the value of art. Watch the full In Conversation on our YouTube channel. @RealGDT pic.twitter.com/XxO05Fpea7

The Pan’s Labyrinth creator has been adamant that the human element of art be preserved — something for which he continued to advocate in his response to the fan, who asked him for his opinion on the “biggest thing lost” when a “computer generates an image instead of a human hand.”

To Del Toro, the “alchemy” of creativity and discovery humans experience when crafting a story or artwork is unachievable by a machine, and many of the best works are often elevated by "accidents" that happen during the creative process.

“The three quarters of the process that gave you the chance to think of the idea that people don't think about without that process,” he answered. “Meaning, AI can get you to the middle really fast, but there's a dialectic with the process that gets you to that top 10%.”

Guillermo del Toro's Frankenstein Images

He went on to use the Pale Man from Pan’s Labyrinth as an example of this, describing how its design was inspired by an unlikely combination of a manta ray and artwork on a poster for Don Coscarelli’s Phantasm.

“We sculpted it as an old man, with a face," he continued. "And then I said, ‘Let's take out the face.’ This happened because I saw a photo of a manta ray and the poster for Don Coscarelli’s Phantasm. That combination, which happened at two different times during a week or a month, are not permutations that are chemically part of an equation. They are alchemy. And then I said, ‘Take out the face,’ and then I said,’ Let's put the eyes on the hands.’ This triangulation happens because I spent a month or two months living with the idea of this creature. And it's not linear.”

Del Toro brought up a conversation he had with Christopher Nolan about The Odyssey (which he previously shared with IGN ), where he asked the director how he’d managed to convincingly pull off Odysseus and his crew braving Poseidon’s stormy seas.

“AI is like a super-fast engine that makes semi-sentient permutations of things that are already done," he said. "Creation is things that have never been done. Coming to exist. And the second thing is the loss of the apprenticeship that one has as an artist. You're never a master; you're always an apprentice. This is a kinship I have with, for example, Chris Nolan. When he showed me The Odyssey , there’s a scene when Matt Damon is floating in the stormy ocean and I asked him — because we were talking about practical effects, and how great it is and that we both always use a maquette or a model — and I asked him, ‘How did you do it?’ He said, ‘We put him in a storm in the ocean.’”

In another delightful anecdote, Del Toro mentioned a past conversation with James Cameron on the set of Terminator 2, describing how Cameron used “accidents” to increase audience immersion and overall believability.

“You're gonna find that 30% of a great image occurs accidentally. You know, either a drop of water hits the lens, or the camera shakes. I remember when in 1993, '94, Jim Cameron and I became friends very fast. And we were looking at Terminator 2 . And he was showing me the scene where Robert Patrick is in the back of the car, and he breaks the window with his arm. And he said, ‘You see those flares?’ I said yeah. He said, ‘We put them there, because the audience thinks an image is real, if you put an accident in it.’ That's true. And I agree. The accident is vital. And the best accidents are things you don't court. They just occur from the interaction with reality,” he said.

We got the chance to speak with Guillermo Del Toro as part of our IGN30 Icons Series, where he revealed how much he loved The Odyssey’s cyclops and told us about his favorite video games — one of which might surprise you .

articles.title: Arthur Morgan's Coughing Fits in Red Dead Redemption 2 Sound So Real Because Actor Roger Clark Was Actually Sick
articles.summary: Red Dead Redemption 2 actor Roger Clark has revealed that Arthur Morgan's gnarly coughing fits were actually recorded when he was sick in real life.
articles.body:
Red Dead Redemption 2 actor Roger Clark has revealed that Arthur Morgan's gnarly coughing fits were actually recorded when he was sick in real life.

I recently interviewed Roger Clark for a YouTube video about how Arthur Morgan from Red Dead Redemption was crafted. During our lengthy conversation, I was able to ask him something I've always wondered: How taxing is it to pretend to violently cough like Arthur does? According to Clark, it's actually not that bad — and in some cases, he wasn't even pretending.

"It's not as bad as you'd think, because I had five years to spread it out," said Clark. "If ever there was a really bad coughing scene, we'd always save it for the end of the day. So, it wasn't as bad as you might think. I had five years to space it out. In five years, there's plenty of colds. There was a lot of data we got that was pretty damn genuine. [...] I'd be like 'Hey, I've got a cold, let me get in there.' And they'd be like, 'Okay.' [...] Nice good bit of phlegm."

There's really no better way to act than to actually experience the scene in your real life. Arthur Morgan is almost partially defined by his coughing; the character contracts Tuberculosis early on in the story after beating a man to death for some money. It's almost a cruel karmic punishment for the life Arthur has led and, depending on the player's choices, they can attempt to redeem the cowboy by helping out others.

As the game goes on, Arthur's coughing gets worse and worse. The player isn't initially aware of why Arthur is so sick, until he starts hacking up his lungs, passes out, and is dragged into a doctor for a proper diagnosis. It's a unique direction to take a game in, and it's part of what makes the story of Red Dead Redemption 2 so memorable.

articles.title: GameStop Is Re-Opening Stores That Previously Closed Down
articles.summary: GameStop is planning to re-open stores that it previously shut down, with one opening its doors this week.
articles.body:
GameStop is planning to re-open stores that it previously shut down, with one opening its doors this week.

The company announced these plans via its social media and revealed that this rollout would begin on September 11. IGN reached out to GameStop to see how many stores are re-opening, and was given the following statement from a GameStop spokesperson:

"The count is: at least one, as of tomorrow. As for the rest, stay tuned."

Your local GameStop is back. Select closed stores are now reopening nationwide starting September 11. pic.twitter.com/OKbS0WAmy4 — GameStop (@gamestop) September 10, 2026

Your local GameStop is back. Select closed stores are now reopening nationwide starting September 11. pic.twitter.com/OKbS0WAmy4

It's slightly amusing to make an announcement like this based on just one store, but for those who want to know the location of this specific shop, you can find it in Ohio at the following address: 4756 Ridge Rd., Suite P22, Brooklyn, OH 44144. GameStop is staying tight lipped as to how many more stores they're planning to resurrect, but hopefully there will be more news soon.

GameStop has had its fair share of struggles over the last half-decade, partially thanks to the rise of digital games. The company has closed over a thousand stores since 2020 and has been cutting costs in other ways over the years. GameStop also briefly killed off Game Informer , a gaming magazine that was owned by the retailer and sold in their stores. Game Informer inevitably found a new owner, but it took nearly a year to bring the magazine back.

Now, GameStop has another obstacle to overcome: the impending death of physical games. PlayStation announced that it is ending support for physical games in 2028 , which seems to suggest the PS6 won't support discs of any kind. The jury is still out on what Xbox plans to do with its next console, but either way, physical gaming media is starting to be phased out by the industry. GameStop may be able to weather this storm, as it has been offering more collectibles and geeky items like Funko Pops for some time now. GameStop is also trying to acquire eBay , which would help diversify the company.

The Xbox Ally is a recent model (October 2025) featuring the AMD Ryzen Z2 A CPU, 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD. The nomenclature might be confusing, but the Xbox Ally is more of an evolution of the the ROG Ally handheld than it is an actual Xbox console. The Xbox Ally runs Windows 11 software, but it boots up straight into the Xbox App. Because you're not loading Windows Explorer, you're freeing up resources typically used for non-gaming background tasks. Not only does this mean you'll get better performance, you'll also get a seamless and tailored user experience.

The Asus ROG Xbox Ally (non-X) model is equipped with a newer generation Ryzen Z2 A processor, which is comparable in performance to the Steam Deck's APU. It's not nearly as powerful as the Ryzen Z2 Extreme found in the higher-end Xbox Ally X, so don't expect high flying performance in demanding games like Crimson Desert or Monster Hunter. However, there are literally thousands of outstanding games available that don't need the most powerful system for you to enjoy.
